Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

vignette: Samantha, a 42-year-old European woman and combat pilot married to her longtime partner, has been struggling with the aftermath of her experiences as a relief worker in a war zone. The traumatic event she experienced there left deep scars that have not healed over time. One cold winter night in her home, Samantha was woken up by a nightmare, and the cold temperature immediately triggered vivid memories of the freezing nights she spent in the war zone, where danger lurked around every corner. As she lay awake, feeling the chill seep into her bones, she found herself unable to shake off the haunting images that flooded her mind. The dreams felt more real than any ordinary memory, as if they were playing out right before her eyes. These triggers didn't just activate painful memories; they also deepened her sense of loss and shattered beliefs. She couldn’t understand how anyone could still trust in a world where such atrocities occurred. This sense of disillusionment made it difficult for Samantha to find meaning or purpose in anything she did, including her work as a pilot. The feeling that nothing mattered anymore led her to engage in compulsive spending—a way to distract herself from the pain and numbness she felt when recalling the event. Samantha’s memory of the traumatic event was particularly vivid and often left her feeling emotionally numb, as if it had happened to someone else. This disconnect made it harder for her to articulate what exactly had occurred; she knew what had happened but could not find words to describe it fully. Her attempts to cope by spending money impulsively only fueled these intrusive thoughts and heightened her vigilance. Her constant threat monitoring included waking up in the middle of the night to check whether anyone was threatening her safety, a behavior that stemmed from feeling vulnerable at all times. This hypervigilance extended beyond just home safety; she felt threatened even by strangers approaching her in ordinary situations. The fear of being caught off guard again led her to avoid watching TV programs or reading about similar events, as doing so often triggered more memories and self-blame. Samantha’s avoidance behaviors further reinforced her sense of identity loss and the belief that nothing mattered anymore. She found herself increasingly isolated from her family and colleagues, unable to share what she had experienced because it felt too painful. This isolation was compounded by her compulsive spending habits, which often led to financial strain and guilt. Over time, Samantha’s work as a pilot became tainted by these memories and fears. The sound of cars reminded her of the constant noise in the war zone, leading her to avoid driving or being near roads whenever possible. This avoidance affected her job performance and strained her relationship with her partner, who could see that something was deeply troubling her but couldn’t fully understand what she was going through. The cumulative effect of these experiences has left Samantha feeling like a different person altogether. Her once clear sense of identity had been shattered by the relentless cycle of triggers, memories, negative appraisals, and maladaptive coping strategies. She began to feel that nothing in her life made sense anymore, and this pervasive sense of loss led her to seek help. Samantha’s current state is marked by a profound fear that she will never be able to reclaim who she was before the traumatic event. At the same time, she holds onto hope that with support and understanding, she can rebuild some semblance of normalcy and regain meaning in her life. The cycle of triggers, memories, negative appraisals, and maladaptive coping strategies has become all-consuming, but she is now ready to confront it head-on.
